records.decision_reason: The LLM converts walkthroughs to predefined action blocks and is quantitatively validated; the interpretive themes come from human reflexive analysis of user-study reflections, making the computational contribution adjacent rather than a core LLM thematic-analysis method.

Research objective.value: Create and evaluate a framework for comparing pacing and experiential balance across open-world game missions.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Mixed-methods evaluation with reflexive thematic analysis of participant reflections.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: GPT-4.1 parses public walkthroughs into a human-defined action-block vocabulary; humans validate an 80-mission gold set and score six MAQV dimensions; experienced users explore a dashboard and researchers conduct the final RTA.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: deductive LLM extraction plus human reflexive thematic interpretation

Public or restricted data.value: public community walkthroughs; derived resources/repository reported

Number of documents.value: approximately 2,200 missions from 20 games; 80 missions in the extraction gold set

Prompting strategy.value: Programmatically constructed deterministic parser prompt with system role, per-game action list, format instructions, and mission text; full specification in Appendix B.

Human role.value: Humans design the action vocabulary/MAQV, double-label a gold set with adjudication, validate dashboard data, and conduct reflexive thematic analysis.

Unit of analysis.value: walkthrough mission step/action block; participant reflection for the human RTA

Generated outputs.value: action sequences, MAQV scores, dashboard visualizations, and human-developed design themes

Automatic metrics.value: step-level extraction metrics, weighted Cohen kappa for MAQV ratings, SUS, UEQ-S, SEQ, and nonparametric comparisons

Human-evaluation design.value: Two authors independently segment 80 missions and a third adjudicates; experienced players/designers verify data and evaluate the interface; researchers separately analyze reflections.

Inter-rater reliability.value: MAQV weighted κ=0.913 (95% CI 0.895–0.929), exact agreement .767; extraction metrics separately reported

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Public walkthrough sources; institutional ethics approval and informed consent for the user study

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report dependence on community walkthrough completeness, a predefined vocabulary, selected game titles, parser errors/granularity, and a small expert-user evaluation.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: strong parser fidelity supports structured extraction only; it does not validate the separately human-constructed reflexive themes or the MAQV framework's construct validity.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: are not used to validate qualitative themes

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Adjacent exemplar of exact-snapshot reporting, adjudicated source-level extraction validation, and correct separation of computational fidelity from interpretive-theme validity.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association advance article, published online 2026
records.decision_reason: The full article develops and evaluates an explicitly human-led GPT-5.2 hybrid deductive–inductive workflow against a Dedoose human analysis with trace-level theme and quotation auditing.

Research objective.value: Develop and evaluate a secure, reproducible human-led LLM workflow for hybrid deductive–inductive analysis of clinical qualitative interviews.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: A human Dedoose analysis served as comparator; GPT-5.2 analyzed transcripts in 13 five-patient/ten-transcript batches through an 11-prompt workflow, produced themes and quotations, and humans audited overlap, deductive provenance, quote fidelity, and run robustness.
Actual operationalized methodology.anchor: official HTML full text, Methods, 11-prompt workflow

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid, predominantly deductive in observed output
Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.anchor: official HTML full text, Results, deductive provenance audit

Domain.value: patient-clinician communication and patient portal/clinical consultation experiences

Number of documents.anchor: official HTML full text, Methods, 122 transcripts

Number of participants.anchor: official HTML full text, Methods, 61 patients

Sensitive-data status.value: HIPAA-sensitive clinical qualitative data processed in ChatGPT Edu
Sensitive-data status.anchor: official HTML full text, Data security

Exact model/version.value: GPT-5.2 in ChatGPT Edu; exact snapshot not reported
Exact model/version.anchor: official HTML full text, Computational workflow

Prompting strategy.value: Eleven sequential prompts with researcher-defined deductive frame, batch processing, code/theme refinement, quotation retrieval, and synthesis.

Human role.value: Humans define the framework, perform reference analysis, inspect every stage, audit themes/quotes, interpret discrepancies, and retain final authority.
Human role.anchor: official HTML full text, Human oversight

Unit of analysis.value: transcript/meaning segment, with five patients per model batch

Generated outputs.value: 63 matched theme pairs plus code/theme structures and supporting quotations
Generated outputs.anchor: official HTML full text, Results, 63 theme pairs

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Model-supplied quotes were checked verbatim against transcripts and classified as verbatim, paraphrased, partial/full hallucination, or truncated.
Evidence/provenance mechanism.anchor: official HTML full text, Quote fidelity audit

Baselines.value: human Dedoose hybrid analysis on the same corpus

Number of runs or seeds.value: three complete repeats on 15 patients/30 transcripts for robustness, plus the main 13-batch run
Number of runs or seeds.anchor: official HTML full text, Robustness analysis

Automatic metrics.value: Jaccard .44–.51 and Hit Rate 1.00 for theme-pair comparison; quote-fidelity proportions
Automatic metrics.anchor: official HTML full text, Results, Jaccard

Human-evaluation design.value: Researchers map theme pairs, audit inductive/deductive origin, and verify every sampled quotation against source text; repeated-run comparison on a subset.

Principal results.value: All human themes were represented at a broad level, but only moderate Jaccard overlap occurred; most supposedly inductive themes were deductive; quotes were 68% verbatim, 20% paraphrased, 6% partial hallucination, 3% full hallucination, and 3% truncated.
Principal results.anchor: official HTML full text, Results, quotation fidelity

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: HIPAA-compliant ChatGPT Edu environment and study ethics/governance procedures were reported.
Ethics and privacy treatment.anchor: official HTML full text, Ethics/Data security

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report one corpus/workflow/model, subjective mapping of theme pairs, batch/context effects, nonzero quote hallucination, and limited generalization.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: Hit Rate 1.00 at broad theme level can coexist with only moderate set overlap, predominantly deductive output, and quote distortion; no metric should collapse those failures into a replication claim.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Material state-of-the-art baseline for trace-level quotation audits, deductive-leakage checks, batching, and repeated-run robustness.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed LAK 2026 conference paper; arXiv manuscript dated 2026-01-18
records.decision_reason: The paper proposes and empirically evaluates reasoning-trace similarity as a triage signal for disagreement in multi-agent qualitative coding, with human reliability and qualitative review.

Research objective.value: Determine whether semantic similarity between coding-agent rationales can surface meaningful disagreement and codebook ambiguity for human review.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Deductive qualitative coding plus human qualitative analysis of agent-reasoning disagreements.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Two DeepSeek-R1 agents independently apply a hybrid human–AI codebook to tutor-dialogue segments and discuss disagreements; a consensus agent adjudicates; BERT cosine similarity compares rationales, and two humans inspect stratified disagreement cases.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: deductive coding with inductive qualitative analysis of disagreement patterns

Number of documents.value: 3,538 dialogue segments from three 60-minute virtual tutoring sessions; 9,746 agent-agent code pairs analyzed

Exact model/version.value: DeepSeek-R1 32B dense variant; BERT embedding model/version not fully specified

Agent roles.value: two independent discussion coders and one consensus agent

Human role.value: Humans previously co-developed the codebook and two coders independently review sampled reasoning-trace cases before consensus.

Unit of analysis.value: tutor–student dialogue segment × code decision and associated rationale pair
Unit of analysis.anchor: treating each segment as an independent

Generated outputs.value: code labels, agent rationales, consensus labels, cosine-similarity disagreement signals, and qualitative codebook-refinement findings

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Repository and reasoning traces link each signal to agent justifications and source segment; context is limited to one segment.

Baselines.value: hybrid human–AI benchmark coding and code-level human inter-coder reliability

Number of runs or seeds.value: stochastic repetitions used to assess similarity-distribution robustness; exact run count not clearly reported in the inspected text

Automatic metrics.value: BERT cosine similarity, Spearman correlation, effect size, confidence intervals, and code-level comparison with human kappa

Human-evaluation design.value: Two humans independently review 15 cases from each of eight within-code categories and selected between-code cases, then reconcile.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: two human coders; expertise not fully characterized

Inter-rater reliability.value: human κ varies by code (examples .80 and .66); agent similarity correlates with label agreement ρ=.54 (95% CI .52–.55)

Principal results.value: Reasoning similarity separated agreement conditions with large effect (d=1.16) and surfaced within-code heterogeneity and fuzzy boundaries, but it is explicitly a triage signal rather than proof that a rationale or label is correct.

Reproducibility resources.value: Public GitHub repository is linked; full model/prompt/run version completeness requires repository audit.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report one dataset/codebook, modest qualitative sample, no systematic rationale-to-definition comparison, limited single-segment context, and no deployed human-facing workflow evaluation.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: same-model agent rationales can be correlated artifacts and are not faithful internal reasoning; cosine similarity predicts agreement, not correctness, interpretive value, or independence.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: should not be mistaken for genuine

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Introduces disagreement-aware human-attention triage, but requires source/codebook grounding and independent correctness/utility checks.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: arXiv preprint submitted 2026-08-04; no peer-reviewed publication identified by 2026-08-24
records.decision_reason: The paper implements a large-scale embedding/clustering plus GPT-5.4 coding workflow, with human refinement and public artifacts, to construct thematic domains from Bluesky posts and executive orders.

Research objective.value: Map themes, sentiment, and temporal dynamics in Trump-related Bluesky discourse and compare them with executive-order themes.
Research objective.anchor: we investigate the online public discourse

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Qwen embeddings, UMAP/HDBSCAN, and Qwen summaries create 4,770 microtopics; GPT-5.4-mini applies 17 seed codes and adds new codes; two researchers merge/refine 344 codes into 14 themes; a parallel procedure yields 19 EO themes.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.anchor: allowing the model to generate new codes

Domain.value: United States political discourse on Bluesky and executive orders

Public or restricted data.value: public Bluesky/API and executive-order data; derived dataset/resources on GitHub
Public or restricted data.anchor: dataset and resources are publicly available

Number of documents.value: 38.5 million posts collected; 30.2 million cleaned English posts; 10,456,083 assigned to 4,770 microtopics; 258 executive orders

Exact model/version.value: Qwen3-Embedding-8B; vLLM-hosted Qwen 30B-A3B variant; GPT-5.4-mini; snapshots not reported

Prompting strategy.value: LLM summaries of up to 100 posts per cluster, then hybrid coding seeded by 17 topic-model codes with permission to induce new codes, followed by theme grouping and human revision.

Human role.value: Two researchers review microtopics/codes, resolve ambiguity, and merge, rename, or revise theme structures.

Unit of analysis.value: post clustered into a microtopic; microtopic summary coded to one dominant overarching theme; executive order

Generated outputs.value: 4,770 microtopics, 344 initial Bluesky codes, 14 Bluesky themes, 24 EO codes, and 19 EO themes

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Public repository, microtopic samples/summaries, partition IDs, code/theme mappings, and supplements; final themes rely on summaries rather than all posts directly.

Baselines.value: Seed codes from an independent topic model and human review; no independent human-only analysis of the full corpus

Automatic metrics.value: silhouette .52–.53, trustworthiness .95, VADER sentiment, and temporal/structural-break analyses

Human-evaluation design.value: Two-researcher iterative validation/refinement; independent blinded evaluation or trace-level coverage sampling not reported

Principal results.value: The workflow produced 14 discourse and 19 EO themes with strong temporal variation; only 10.5M of 30.2M cleaned posts entered identifiable microtopics.
Principal results.anchor: remaining posts were treated as unclustered

Reproducibility resources.value: Dataset, supplements, and code repositories are linked publicly; exact hosted-model snapshots and all stochastic settings are incomplete.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report keyword/platform/language selection, Bluesky population skew, VADER limitations, clustering/unassigned-post loss, and interpretation dependence.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: themes are induced primarily from cluster summaries and 65% of cleaned posts are unassigned, so downstream salience and omission claims require a documented coverage/trace audit.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Scale benchmark for hierarchical provenance and hybrid induction, with a material warning about coverage loss between documents, clusters, summaries, codes, and themes.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access Studies in Health Technology and Informatics proceedings chapter, 2026
records.decision_reason: The case study compares Microsoft Copilot and researcher qualitative-content-analysis categories on the same sampled DNAR responses and explicitly examines divergent interpretive emphasis.

Research objective.value: Explore Copilot as an interpretive partner for identifying problems in do-not-attempt-resuscitation order making.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Interpretative framework and qualitative content analysis.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: From 893 survey responses, 100 were analyzed by Copilot and the same two researchers; each produced 15 categories, frequencies were placed on a three-level scale, and researchers reflexively compared meaning, trust, and authority.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: inductive content categorization with comparative synthesis

Number of participants.value: 524 healthcare professionals contributed 893 responses; 100 views sampled

Human role.value: Two researchers conduct the human analysis, interpret both sets of categories, and perform reflexive synthesis; responsibility remains human.

Unit of analysis.value: healthcare professional response to one DNAR-problem question

Generated outputs.value: 15 Copilot and 15 researcher thematic categories with frequency bands

Automatic metrics.value: category reference counts grouped into high/medium/low frequency; no agreement coefficient

Human-evaluation design.value: Reflexive author comparison of category emphasis; independent/blinded matching not reported

Principal results.value: Both yielded 15 categories, but Copilot emphasized patient/family roles and practical issues while researchers emphasized communication/documentation; authors retain deeper interpretation as a human task.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Ethical clinical context is central; original survey governance is referenced, but platform data-handling/version details are not reported in the chapter.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors note small selected sample, one question, single chatbot, descriptive frequency comparison, and need for larger/diverse datasets.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: no prompt, version, sampling procedure, source-to-category mapping, independent evaluator, or formal agreement measure makes the AI–human comparison difficult to reproduce and vulnerable to author-confirmation bias.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Illustrates divergent emphasis and epistemic-authority questions, but is a weak benchmark without trace and workflow reporting.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: arXiv preprint under review, submitted January 2026; no peer-reviewed publication identified by 2026-08-24
records.decision_reason: This process study observes three experienced researchers using a purpose-built GPT-4 Turbo inductive-analysis scaffold and analyzes their complete interaction/revision traces.

Research objective.value: Explain how experienced qualitative researchers exercise judgment and epistemic authority while using ITA-GPT for inductive thematic analysis.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Human–AI collaborative inductive thematic analysis grounded in reflexive thematic analysis and verbatim/process coding.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Three researchers each analyze an assigned Ghanaian teacher-education transcript through staged familiarization, in-vivo/gerund coding and themes; chat histories, tracked revisions, comments, and memos are then process-coded to study human interventions.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: inductive, with a methodologically prestructured scaffold

Domain.value: Ghanaian teacher education and lecturer recruitment/professional experience

Number of documents.value: three interview transcripts, one per analytic participant

Number of participants.value: three experienced qualitative researchers as analytic participants; source-interview participant count not reported

Exact model/version.value: GPT-4 Turbo API; snapshot not reported

Prompting strategy.value: Interactive system prompt enforces staged consent/progression, verbatim and gerund coding, transcript-coverage checks, reflexive memos, and provisional theme generation.

Human role.value: Researchers authorize each phase and modify, delete, reject, insert, and comment on provisional outputs; humans remain final interpreters.

Unit of analysis.value: source-transcript segment and human–AI analytic action/revision

Generated outputs.value: verbatim/gerund codes, code families/themes, summaries, memos, reflexive records, coverage checks, and revision traces

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Exact participant text in multi-column tables, complete shared chat histories, tracked changes, transcript coverage checks, and reflexive memos

Baselines.value: No independent human-only or autonomous-model baseline; cross-researcher process comparison

Human-evaluation design.value: Qualitative process analysis of all three analysts' logged revisions and reflections

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: three researchers with prior qualitative-research/coding experience

Principal results.value: Researchers valued procedural scaffolding and exact in-vivo codes but repeatedly corrected literal, emotionally neutral, or institutionally naive abstractions; five recurring human actions operationalized authority.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Previously approved Ghanaian interview project with consent; transcripts reused solely as analytic material; human oversight and accountability foregrounded.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report only three expert analysts/three transcripts in one education context, a purpose-built prompt/model, researcher-as-participant effects, and no performance or time comparator.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: analysts did not work on the same transcripts, so cross-coder differences confound person and corpus; authors built the tool/framework and analyzed favorable process evidence without independent audit.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Material empirical source for revision ledgers, reflexive prompts, coverage gates, in-vivo anchoring, and explicit human veto/authority.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access Qualitative Health Research article, first published online 2025 and assigned to 2026 volume/issue
records.decision_reason: The study compares Claude 3.5 Sonnet's category coding with the original human immersion–crystallization analysis of the same Hebrew medical-student narratives.

Research objective.value: Evaluate whether an LLM can reproduce contextual coding of medical-student narratives and identify where human interpretation remains necessary.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Immersion/crystallization manual analysis and contextual/thematic narrative coding.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Original researchers built a consensus codebook; Claude 3.5 Sonnet coded 166 narratives under category-specific closed and open prompts; outputs were compared with human labels using kappa/accuracy/F1 and qualitatively reviewed by original analysts.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: primarily deductive/contextual model coding against human-developed categories, with one open specialty category

Domain.value: medical students' difficult clinician–patient communication narratives

Model family.value: Anthropic Claude; OpenAI GPT tested on samples

Exact model/version.value: Claude 3.5 Sonnet via Claude.ai in August 2024; OpenAI model/version for sample tests not reported

Prompting strategy.value: Category-specific foundational prompt requesting CSV rows; iterative refinement after qualitative comparison; one category switched to open-ended extraction.

Human role.value: Original analysts build reference categories, design/refine prompts, review differences, and supply medical-context interpretation.
Human role.anchor: involved in the original manual human analysis

Generated outputs.value: closed-category labels and open-ended physician-specialty labels

Automatic metrics.value: Cohen kappa, accuracy, F1, and category-wise discrepancy percentages

Human-evaluation design.value: Original human analysts qualitatively inspect gaps after metric comparison; no independent blinded evaluator

Inter-rater reliability.value: category-specific kappa ranged from near chance for subtle categories to high for explicit attributes; exact table values reported

Principal results.value: The model closely matched explicit information but struggled with surprise, relationship identity, setting, and other context/emotion requiring medical or narrative inference.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Tel Aviv ethics approval, consent, de-identification, secondary-use consultation, and model choice informed by retention/training policies

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report one model/interface/language/domain, reference-code subjectivity, no fine-tuning, no timing comparison, and limited transfer to open interpretive theme development.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: prompt refinement after original analysts inspected errors risks test-set leakage; human labels are consensus interpretations, not an objective gold standard.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Useful category-difficulty evidence: explicit extraction success does not generalize to emotion, context, or interpretive meaning.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access Medical Science Educator article, accepted 2025-11-13 and in the 2026 collection
records.decision_reason: The study tests three increasingly supervised ChatGPT-3.5 coding protocols, each in three repeated runs, against manual thematic labels on 343 responses.

Research objective.value: Evaluate how prompt/instruction design affects ChatGPT thematic-code application compared with manual graders.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Inductive theme development followed by deductive multi-label thematic coding.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: ChatGPT helped two authors derive/refine 14 themes from 30 responses; humans then coded all 343; ChatGPT-3.5 applied those themes under definition-only, 25-example few-shot, and interactive definition-revision protocols, each repeated three times.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid, but the evaluated task is deductive code application
Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.anchor: mainly focused on AI’s ability to perform a deductive

Domain.value: first-year medical students' anticipatory reflections on cadaveric dissection

Public or restricted data.value: restricted educational responses; available on request
Public or restricted data.anchor: Data used in this study are available upon request

Exact model/version.value: ChatGPT 3.5 free interface; snapshot not reported

Prompting strategy.value: Three protocols: definitions only; 25 labeled examples; or sequential feedback on 25 examples that edits definitions before coding the remainder.

Human role.value: Two authors curate AI-suggested themes, establish >90% pilot agreement, manually code half the corpus each, and provide feedback for Method 3.

Generated outputs.value: 14-theme assignments under three prompting methods across three runs
Generated outputs.anchor: Each method of instructing ChatGPT was repeated three times

Baselines.value: manual author coding using the 14-theme codebook

Automatic metrics.value: total/marked accuracy and precision, Cohen kappa, sensitivity/specificity, ANOVA on ranks, and Marascuilo comparisons

Human-evaluation design.value: Two-human pilot reliability check on 20 responses; full reference corpus split between graders rather than double-coded
Human-evaluation design.anchor: 20 of the responses were coded by both observers

Inter-rater reliability.value: human pilot agreement >90%; human–AI agreement 81.7/82.2/83.9%, κ=.43/.47/.50; sensitivity <60%, specificity >85%

Principal results.value: More interactive supervision raised accuracy but reduced run-to-run precision; prompt effects varied by theme, and culturally/physically nuanced themes had low marked accuracy.
Principal results.anchor: Method 3 had a greater total and marked accuracy

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: University of Cincinnati IRB #2023-0814; response data available only on request

Reproducibility resources.value: Supplementary theme definitions and protocol detail; exact snapshot and raw run outputs not reported

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report obsolete single model, AI involvement in initial theme creation favoring later AI matching, one dataset, and focus on deductive rather than full thematic analysis.
Author-reported limitations.anchor: utilizing ChatGPT to identify the themes may have placed bias

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: model-assisted creation of the reference codebook is dependence leakage; overall accuracy is inflated by true negatives, and most responses were not independently double-coded by humans.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Material evidence for prompt-treatment ablations and repeated-run precision, plus warnings about leakage and class-imbalance metrics.
